name: John Wesley Dobbs
bio: Known as the 'unofficial mayor of Auburn Avenue,' Dobbs was a prominent civic leader and Grand Master of Georgia's Prince Hall Masons. He championed Black voter registration and political empowerment in Atlanta.

name: Irene Thompson Dobbs
bio: Wife of John Wesley Dobbs and matriarch of a family that would produce educators, diplomats, and civil rights leaders across multiple generations.

name: Alonzo Herndon
bio: Born into slavery, Herndon became Atlanta's wealthiest Black citizen. He founded Atlanta Life Insurance Company in 1905 and built a barber shop empire that served white Atlanta's elite.

name: Adrienne McNeil Herndon
bio: Acclaimed actress and elocutionist who taught drama at Atlanta University. She was one of the first Black women to earn national recognition in the performing arts.

name: Antoine Graves
bio: A founding member of South-View Cemetery Association in 1886. Graves was among the group of Black civic leaders who established the cemetery so that African Americans could be buried with dignity.

name: Albert Watts
bio: One of the original founders of South-View Cemetery. Watts helped organize the purchase of the original nine acres of land that would become the cemetery.

name: James Tate
bio: A minister and community leader who was instrumental in the early growth of South-View Cemetery. He helped expand the cemetery's reach to serve the broader Atlanta Black community.

name: Selena Sloan Butler
bio: Founder of the first Black parent-teacher association in the United States (1911). Butler was a tireless advocate for education and community welfare in Atlanta.

name: Henry Rutherford Butler
bio: One of Atlanta's first Black physicians. Dr. Butler was a prominent figure in the city's Black professional class and co-founded several community organizations.

name: Mary Carter Smith
bio: A schoolteacher who taught in Atlanta's segregated public schools for over 30 years, educating generations of Black children during the Jim Crow era.

name: Robert Carter
bio: A skilled carpenter and builder who helped construct several churches and schools in Atlanta's Black neighborhoods during the early 20th century.

name: Ella Mae Carter
bio: A domestic worker and church deaconess who organized mutual aid societies in her neighborhood, helping families during times of hardship.

name: Rev. William Parks
bio: Pastor of a prominent Baptist church in Atlanta's West Side. Parks was known for his fiery sermons advocating for racial justice and economic self-sufficiency.

name: Lucius Harper
bio: Owner of a successful Black-owned grocery on Auburn Avenue. Harper employed dozens of young Black men and women and was an active member of the local business league.

name: Dorothy Harper
bio: A midwife who delivered hundreds of babies in the Atlanta Black community. Known for her tireless service, she often traveled on foot to reach families in need.

name: George A. Towns
bio: Professor of English and pedagogy at Atlanta University for over 50 years. Towns was one of the first Black graduates of Harvard University and a contemporary of W.E.B. Du Bois.

name: Josephine Murphy
bio: A seamstress and labor organizer who advocated for fair wages for Black domestic and garment workers in Atlanta during the 1930s and 1940s.

name: Thomas Grant
bio: A Pullman porter who used his position to distribute Black newspapers and information about civil rights organizing across the South.
